Title: Vagus nerve stimulation has antidepressant effects in the kainic acid model for temporal lobe epilepsy.

Journal/Date: Brain stimulation (2015)

MeSH Keywords: Anhedonia, Animals, Choice Behavior, Major Depressive Disorder, Disease Models, Animal, Epilepsy, Temporal Lobe, Kainic Acid, Male


--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: Depression is the most common psychiatric comorbidity in epilepsy patients. The lack of success with current pharmacological interventions for this patient population, highlights the importance of optimizing non-pharmacological neuromodulatory treatments such as vagus nerve stimulation (VNS). Studies on the antidepressant effect of VNS in epilepsy patients may be confounded by concurrent anti-epileptic drug therapy. To date, studies in epilepsy models overcoming this problem are lacking.
[OBJECTIVE]: We investigated whether VNS affects anhedonia, a key symptom of major depression, in the kainic acid rat model for temporal lobe epilepsy.
[METHODS]: Anhedonia was assessed in kainic acid (KA) and saline (SAL) injected rats using the saccharin preference test (SPT). To exclude differences in taste perception, the quinine aversion test (QAT) was performed. Both groups were randomly subdivided in a VNS and a SHAM group, yielding 4 experimental arms: KA-VNS, KA-SHAM, SAL-VNS and SAL-SHAM. Both VNS groups received 2 weeks of VNS, while the SHAM groups were not stimulated. Thereafter, the SPT and QAT were repeated.
[RESULTS]: Saccharin preference was significantly reduced in the KA compared to the SAL rats (P < 0.05), without differences in quinine aversion. Two weeks of VNS significantly increased the saccharin preference in the KA-VNS group (P < 0.05), while it had no effect on quinine aversion. No effects of VNS or SHAM were found in the other groups.
[CONCLUSION]: The KA rats displayed anhedonia which was significantly decreased by VNS, indicating that this neuromodulatory treatment could likewise diminish depressive symptoms in patients suffering from temporal lobe epilepsy and comorbid depression.

key_findings.finding: A direct preclinical study in the kainic-acid rat model of temporal-lobe epilepsy (PMID 25444592; Brain Stimulation, 2015) randomized KA- and saline-injected male rats to 2 weeks of VNS or sham stimulation (four arms: KA-VNS, KA-sham, saline-VNS, saline-sham). The study assessed anhedonia with saccharin preference and controlled for taste perception with quinine aversion. KA rats had reduced saccharin preference without altered quinine aversion, and VNS significantly restored saccharin preference in KA rats without affecting quinine aversion; no VNS/sham effects were observed in saline controls. This directly supports an antidepressant-like, specifically anti-anhedonic, effect of VNS in the KA epilepsy model.

observations: In male rats with kainic-acid-induced temporal-lobe epilepsy, 2 weeks of VNS increased saccharin preference versus sham stimulation, indicating reversal of anhedonia-like behavior; quinine aversion was unchanged.
The study used four randomized groups: KA-VNS, KA-sham, saline-VNS, and saline-sham; no VNS effect was observed in saline controls.

source_tools.relevance: Direct primary study of VNS in the kainic-acid epilepsy model.

entities.name: VNS anti-anhedonia in KA epilepsy
observations: VNS restored reduced saccharin preference in kainic-acid-treated rats without changing quinine aversion, supporting an antidepressant-like anti-anhedonic effect rather than altered taste perception.

entities.name: Kainic acid epilepsy model
observations: Kainic acid-induced rat model of temporal-lobe epilepsy was associated with reduced saccharin preference, used as an anhedonia-like phenotype.
The identified evidence base contains one clearly direct KA-plus-VNS preclinical study; other cited evidence is secondary or from different contexts.
